description_ru: Юмористический рассказ от первого лица о сборке мебели из плоской упаковки, где инструкция без слов оказывается испытанием для брака и рассудка.
text:
It arrived in a flat cardboard box the size of a coffin, which should have been a warning, since I had ordered a wardrobe, and wardrobes, in my experience, are not a thing that one buries. The label on the side said SKRÖMBEL, followed by a string of numbers, a picture of a smiling family who had clearly never opened one, and the legend "Easy to assemble in under an hour." Reader, I have since learned that in the dialect of the furniture trade, "easy" means "theoretically possible" and "an hour" means "the better part of your marriage."

I opened the box on a Saturday morning, with the buoyant optimism of a man who has recently watched a video of a carpenter. Inside lay forty-three panels, a bag of something that rattled, a second bag of something that rattled differently, a small hexagonal key of the sort used to torture dentists, and a booklet of instructions entirely devoid of words. This was, I was informed by the company's website, a deliberate policy. The instructions had been drawn by a team of illustrators in order to be "linguistically universal," a phrase that I now understand to mean "comprehensible to nobody in any language whatever."

The booklet began cheerfully. Page one showed a small, bald, expressionless man, whom I came to call Gunnar, holding a panel and smiling at it with the warmth of a person who has never been alone with a wardrobe. Page two showed Gunnar inserting a wooden dowel into a hole. I located the dowel, which was the size of a cigarette and appeared to have been designed by an intelligence unfamiliar with cigarettes, and I located the hole, which was precisely the size of a different dowel. This was the point at which Gunnar and I parted company, though he did not know it.

By ten o'clock I had established, by painful experiment, that panel F was upside down, that panel G was inside out and that panels H, J and the one I privately called Kevin were not, as far as I could determine, in the box at all. By eleven I was crawling on the carpet, sweating freely and addressing a piece of chipboard in the tone one normally reserves for a disobedient spaniel. By noon, I had discovered that the second bag of rattling items contained a set of fifty-two screws, of which the instructions made use of fifty-one, so that I had inherited, as it were, a screw in reserve, like a spare tyre for a life I had not yet lived.

My wife, a woman of enormous practicality, came in at half past twelve with a cup of tea and an expression of detached amusement. She stood in the doorway and surveyed the scene: the carpet carpeted with panels, the husband crouched in the middle like a hermit crab, the little hexagonal key clenched between his teeth. "How's it going?" she asked. "Splendidly," I said, in a voice that I recognised, with some dismay, as my father's. "It's going splendidly. I'm almost at the part where it starts to look like furniture." She nodded gravely and withdrew, closing the door with the quiet respect that one extends to the bereaved.

At two o'clock a breakthrough occurred. I discovered, by a process of elimination and a short, undignified wrestle, that if one ignores the pictures altogether, and relies instead on the shape of the pieces, the thing begins to resemble a wardrobe. A side panel snapped into a slot. A shelf slid obligingly into place. For ten minutes, I experienced the intoxicating sensation of competence, a feeling akin to that of an explorer who has found the source of the Nile and is wondering where to put the flag. Then I attached the door, stepped back and noticed that it was on the inside.

I will not describe the next hour. Suffice it to say that I disassembled the door, disassembled the side panel to which it was attached, disassembled the shelf that had lodged behind the side panel, and discovered, to my deep embarrassment, that the dowel with which I had begun was still lying, perfectly intact, in my trouser pocket. It had been there since the morning, a small cylindrical reproach. I put it in the bag labelled "Spare," where, I suppose, it joined the others, and the screw, and a faint feeling of having been cheated by Sweden.

By five, the thing stood upright. It was, I confess, a handsome object, tall and solemn, and slightly resembled a bishop. It also leaned, very gently, to the left, in the manner of a man contemplating a distant and rather disappointing horizon. I placed a spirit level on its top, and observed the bubble drift to one side and remain there, with the air of one who has no intention of cooperating. I took this, quite reasonably, as a matter of artistic expression, and decided that the wardrobe had personality.

That evening, my wife and I hung clothes in it. Within an hour the wardrobe had begun, with a faint creak, to express opinions. It creaked when we opened the door, creaked when we closed it, and, in the small hours, creaked for no discernible reason, with a long, melancholy groan that seemed to originate from the soul of the particleboard itself. We named it Skrömbel, partly in honour of the label and partly because it seemed to us that anything so bad-tempered ought to have a name that sounds like a rumble of indigestion.

It stands there still, three years later, a monument to my patience and to the structural ambition of the Swedish nation. It has survived two removals, a minor earthquake and a toddler's decision to climb it, and nothing, including my sense of pride, has ever dented it. Visitors compliment its lines. I tell them that I made it myself, and watch, with quiet delight, as their expression passes from admiration to concern, as they notice the leftover screw that I have kept, for reasons of sentiment, in a small dish on the mantelpiece.

Last month, I received an email from the manufacturer, offering me a discount on a bookcase called the Glörp. I did not reply, but I read it, for some minutes, with the rapt attention of a man who is deciding whether to remarry. The little hexagonal key, I note, is still in the drawer. And on certain evenings, when the house is quiet and the wardrobe creaks, I take out the booklet and look at Gunnar, smiling blankly at his panel, and I think: you, sir, knew all along.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: Дифтонг: начинайте с округлённого «о» и скользите к «и»; второй элемент короткий.
Губы вытянуты вперёд трубочкой, зубов не касаются; не русское «в».
Кончик языка между зубами, без голоса; не заменяйте на «с», «ф» или «т».
Начальные p, t, k произносятся с лёгким выдохом, как будто после них тихое «х»; в русском такого придыхания нет.

questions.question: What was unusual about the instruction booklet?
questions.answer: It had no words, only pictures.

questions.question: What mistake did the narrator make with the door?
questions.answer: He attached it on the inside.
